error_modes.label: ALTITUDE CONTROL THROUGH THE PITCH OUT

texts.0: SP, due to attention held outside on the leader instead of returning to the altimeter after the roll-in, did not maintain the pitch out altitude and allowed the aircraft to descend throughout the turn. The aircraft passed 400 feet below the pattern altitude with the descent still developing and no correction started. IP took the controls and recovered the aircraft to the pattern altitude before rollout on downwind.
texts.1: SP, due to a pitch attitude that was not reset against the bank after establishing the pitch out, did not hold the pitch out altitude and let the aircraft settle in the turn. The deviation reached 300 feet low, at the limit of the tolerance for the maneuver, and stopped only after IP called the altitude twice. SP regained the pattern altitude on downwind, but the correction came from verbal prompting rather than from own cross-check.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed return of the cross-check to the altimeter after rolling into the pitch out, initially allowed the aircraft to descend about 200 feet below the pattern altitude. SP identified the deviation while still in the turn and corrected back inside the tolerance before rolling out on downwind. No prompting or intervention by IP was required.
texts.3: SP maintained the pitch out altitude throughout the turn with deviations contained inside 150 feet. The altimeter cross-check ran continuously against the bank and the aircraft was level at the pattern altitude at rollout on downwind. Corrections were small, early and made on SP own initiative.
texts.4: SP flew the pitch out with the altitude held essentially constant, the deviation never exceeding a few tens of feet at any point in the turn. Pitch was traded against bank with no perceptible settle at either the roll-in or the rollout. The pattern altitude was regained and held with negligible error.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the pitch out altitude within standards, but every turn was flown with the same low bias, reaching about 130 feet before being corrected on the downwind leg. The trend is a repeated settle at the roll-in that is caught late instead of being prevented. SP is expected to set and hold the pitch attitude against the bank as it is established, so that the altitude stays within a considerably tighter band.

error_modes.label: AIRSPEED CONTROL DURING THE PITCH OUT

texts.0: SP, due to power left at the transit setting when the pitch out was executed, did not maintain the pre-determined airspeed required of formation members during the pitch out. The aircraft accelerated to 35 knots above the briefed figure and the excess was still increasing on downwind. IP had to direct the power reduction and then reduce the power personally to bring the aircraft back inside the pattern speed.
texts.1: SP, due to the power reduction being made only after the bank was fully established rather than with it, did not hold the pre-determined pitch out airspeed. The aircraft reached 20 knots fast, at the limit of the tolerance, and was brought back only after IP called the airspeed. The speed was inside standards on downwind, but the correction was produced by the prompt and not by SP own scan.
texts.2: SP, due to a power setting selected without reference to the briefed pitch out figure, initially allowed the airspeed to build about 15 knots above the pre-determined value. SP noted the trend on the airspeed indicator during the turn and reset the power in good time, recovering the briefed speed before rollout on downwind without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained the pre-determined pitch out airspeed with deviations contained inside 10 knots throughout the maneuver. Power was reduced together with the roll-in and adjusted in small increments as the bank was held. The briefed pattern speed was established on downwind without any correction being called.
texts.4: SP flew the pitch out with the airspeed pinned to the pre-determined figure, the deviation remaining within a very few knots from roll-in to rollout. Power was led rather than chased, so no speed excursion ever developed. The pattern speed on downwind was exactly the briefed value.
texts.marginal: SP held the pitch out airspeed within standards, but the aircraft was consistently about 9 knots fast from the roll-in to the rollout on downwind. The trend is a habitual late power reduction that leaves the speed at the outer edge of the acceptable band on every pitch out. SP is expected to reduce power together with the roll-in so that the pre-determined airspeed is achieved from the start of the turn.

error_modes.label: EXIT HEADING AND ROLLOUT ON DOWNWIND

texts.0: SP, due to the rollout being flown by looking at the runway rather than by anticipating the downwind heading, did not stop the turn on the required exit heading. The aircraft rolled out 18 degrees through the downwind heading and continued to diverge from the runway track. IP directed the recovery turn and then took the controls to reestablish the aircraft on the downwind leg.
texts.1: SP, due to the roll-out being started at the exit heading instead of being led, did not achieve the required exit heading of the pitch out. The aircraft settled 10 degrees off the downwind heading, at the limit of the tolerance, and was realigned only after IP called the heading. The correction restored the track but was produced by the prompt rather than by SP own cross-check.
texts.2: SP, due to a roll rate that was reduced too late in the recovery from the pitch out bank, initially rolled out about 8 degrees off the required downwind heading. SP recognized the offset immediately on the heading indicator and corrected onto the exit heading inside the tolerance before the spacing check, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP rolled out of the pitch out on the required exit heading with the deviation contained inside 5 degrees. The roll-out was led so that the wings came level as the downwind heading was reached. The aircraft was tracking the downwind leg without any subsequent heading correction.
texts.4: SP stopped the pitch out precisely on the required exit heading, with the residual deviation of the order of one or two degrees. The roll-out was anticipated exactly, so the wings came level and the heading stabilized in the same instant. No corrective input was needed on the downwind leg.
texts.marginal: SP achieved the exit heading of the pitch out within standards, but every rollout finished about 5 degrees outside the downwind heading in the same direction. The trend is a roll-out that is consistently started late and then patched with a small corrective turn. SP is expected to lead the roll-out from the pitch out bank so that the exit heading is achieved directly rather than corrected afterwards.

error_modes.label: RESPONSE TO LEADER COMMAND AND PITCH OUT TIMING

texts.0: SP, due to the pitch out signal being expected on the radio while the leader gave it visually, did not execute the pitch out following the leader command as laid down in the Techniques and Procedures Manual. The turn was started more than eight seconds late and the resulting interval was far outside anything usable for the pattern. IP had to command the turn and then intervene on the controls to salvage a workable spacing.
texts.1: SP, due to hesitation in confirming the leader command before acting on it, did not execute the pitch out in a timely manner. The turn was initiated some three seconds late and the interval finished at the outer limit of what the pattern allows, being adjusted only after IP called for the turn. The maneuver was completed to standard, but the timing was driven by IP prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to the head being inside the cockpit at the moment the leader command was given, initially started the pitch out slightly late. SP recognized the delay at once, adjusted the bank and the power inside the briefed limits, and restored the interval to the required value before the downwind spacing check without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP executed the pitch out following the leader command, in the manner prescribed by the Techniques and Procedures Manual. The turn was started without perceptible delay and the resulting interval was the briefed one. No adjustment to the timing was required at any stage.
texts.4: SP executed the pitch out on the leader command with immediate and precise response, the turn starting exactly on the signal. The interval produced matched the briefed figure with negligible error and required no subsequent adjustment. SP anticipation of the command point was evident throughout.
texts.marginal: SP executed the pitch out following the leader command within standards, but consistently a beat behind the signal on each repetition. The trend is an interval built slightly long every time, absorbed later by adjustments on the downwind leg. SP is expected to act on the leader command as it is given so that the interval is correct from the roll-in.

texts.0: SP, due to the briefed bank value not being flown against the attitude indicator, did not maintain the pre-determined bank required of formation members during the pitch out. The bank was some 20 degrees shallower than briefed and the spacing produced was unusable for the pattern. IP took the controls, reestablished the correct bank and rebuilt the interval before the downwind leg.
texts.1: SP, due to a bank that was allowed to relax as attention moved back to the leader, did not hold the pre-determined pitch out bank. The bank wandered around the briefed value and the resulting spacing finished at the limit of what the pattern allows, being corrected only after IP called the bank angle. The interval was recovered, but through prompting rather than through SP own cross-check.
texts.2: SP, due to a roll-in that was stopped short of the briefed value, initially flew the pitch out with insufficient bank and a spacing trend toward the long side. SP identified the shallow bank on the attitude indicator early in the turn, increased it to the pre-determined value and restored the interval inside acceptable limits without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained the pre-determined bank throughout the pitch out and produced the briefed spacing. The bank was set at the roll-in and held constant until the roll-out was led for the exit heading. The interval on downwind matched the briefed figure with no adjustment required.
texts.4: SP held the pre-determined pitch out bank with negligible variation from roll-in to roll-out, producing spacing that matched the briefed interval exactly. The bank was established in a single positive input and required no trimming during the turn. The resulting interval needed no correction whatsoever on the downwind leg.
texts.marginal: SP flew the pitch out with the pre-determined bank within standards, but the bank was consistently a few degrees shallow and the interval consistently at the long end of the acceptable range. The trend is a spacing that is workable but always has to be closed later in the pattern. SP is expected to set the full briefed bank at the roll-in so that the interval is generated by the pitch out itself.

error_modes.label: SMOOTHNESS AND SOLIDITY OF AIRCRAFT CONTROL

texts.0: SP, due to control inputs applied in large uncoordinated steps rather than in a continuous manner, did not control the aircraft in a smooth and solid way during the pitch out. The roll-in was abrupt, the ball was displaced for the whole turn and the load factor oscillated noticeably. IP took the controls to stabilize the aircraft and complete the maneuver.
texts.1: SP, due to overcontrolling in roll and then chasing the resulting pitch changes, did not fly the pitch out in a smooth and solid way. The turn was flown with repeated coarse corrections in roll and pitch and settled down only after IP called for smaller inputs. Control of the aircraft was regained, but only on verbal direction from IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a rudder input that did not accompany the initial roll, initially flew the pitch out out of balance with a visible ball displacement. SP recognized the uncoordinated entry, coordinated the rudder with the aileron and flew the remainder of the turn smoothly and firmly without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid way throughout the pitch out. Roll, pitch and rudder inputs were coordinated, the flight path was continuous and the aircraft remained in balance from entry to rollout. No coarse or corrective input was observed.
texts.4: SP flew the pitch out with control inputs of exceptional smoothness and precision, the aircraft tracking a continuous flight path with the ball centered throughout. Roll-in and roll-out were single positive movements with no subsequent correction. Any deviation from the ideal flight path was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid way within standards, but the roll rate at the entry varied noticeably between repetitions and small ball displacements appeared at each roll-out. The trend is inconsistency in the entry and exit inputs rather than any loss of control. SP is expected to standardize the roll rate and coordinate the rudder so that every pitch out is flown to the same smooth pattern.

texts.0: SP, due to reluctance to admit loss of visual contact and make the required call, did not handle the blind situation correctly when the leader was lost against the ground background in the pitch out. SP continued to turn toward the last known position of the leader with no call made and no deconfliction action taken. IP made the blind call and took the controls to separate the aircraft from the element.
texts.1: SP, due to hesitation in using the prescribed terminology once visual contact was lost, did not handle the blind situation in a timely manner. The blind call was made some five seconds late and only after IP prompted for it, and the deconfliction turn followed the call rather than accompanying it. Visual contact was regained, but the sequence was driven by IP direction.
texts.2: SP, due to visual contact being broken as the leader passed through the canopy bow during the pitch out, was momentarily blind in the turn. SP made the blind call promptly in the prescribed terminology, held the briefed altitude for deconfliction and regained visual contact before the rollout, with no IP intervention required.
texts.3: SP handled the blind situation correctly and in a timely manner when visual contact was momentarily lost during the pitch out. The call was made immediately in the prescribed terminology, the briefed deconfliction responsibilities were applied and visual contact was regained. The pattern sequence continued without disruption.
texts.4: SP handled the loss of visual contact with exemplary decisiveness, the blind call and the deconfliction action being taken in the same instant the leader was lost from sight. The call carried the position and altitude information needed for the leader to resolve the situation immediately. Visual contact was regained with negligible loss of pattern discipline.
texts.marginal: SP handled the blind situation within standards, but the call was made only after a perceptible pause and in phraseology that had to be repeated to be understood. The trend is a correct action taken with hesitation at exactly the moment when speed matters most. SP is expected to make the blind call immediately and in standard terminology as soon as visual contact is lost.

error_modes.label: SPACING ASSESSMENT AND CORRECTION ON DOWNWIND

texts.0: SP, due to a mental picture of the pattern built entirely on the leader position and not on the geometry of the runway, did not assess the spacing produced by the pitch out at any point on the downwind leg. The interval remained far outside the briefed value with no correction attempted and the pattern sequence was compromised. IP had to direct the extension of the downwind leg and then take the controls to reestablish a usable interval.
texts.1: SP, due to situational awareness being reduced to the leader alone with no reference to the runway abeam position, did not assess the spacing after the pitch out. The interval finished at the limit of what the pattern allows and was corrected only after IP called for a power adjustment on the downwind leg. The correction restored the sequence but originated with IP.
texts.2: SP, due to the spacing check being delayed until well after the rollout, initially carried an interval noticeably shorter than the briefed one. SP detected the closure against the leader on the downwind leg, adjusted power and track in good time and restored the correct interval before the base turn, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP assessed the spacing generated by the pitch out immediately on rolling out on downwind and maintained the briefed interval. The assessment was made against both the leader and the runway abeam position, and the small power adjustment required was applied early. The pattern sequence proceeded exactly as briefed.
texts.4: SP assessed and controlled the spacing with exceptional accuracy, the interval matching the briefed figure from the rollout to the base turn. The picture was cross-checked continuously against the leader and the runway, so no adjustment beyond a minimal power change was ever needed. The pattern sequence was flown with negligible deviation.
texts.marginal: SP assessed and maintained the spacing within standards, but the interval was recognized late on every circuit and always needed a power change on the downwind leg to bring it back. The trend is an awareness of the spacing that is reconstructed after the rollout rather than carried through the pitch out. SP is expected to judge the interval during the turn so that the downwind leg begins with the briefed spacing already established.

error_modes.label: CLEARING AND DECONFLICTION THROUGH THE PITCH OUT

texts.0: SP, due to attention captured entirely by the leader aircraft at the expense of the visual scan of the pattern, did not clear the turn direction before rolling into the pitch out. Another aircraft established on the downwind leg went unseen and the turn was continued toward it. IP called the traffic and took the controls to break off the turn and reestablish separation.
texts.1: SP, due to the whole visual scan being locked on the leader during the run-in, did not clear the pattern before the pitch out. The clearing turn of the head was made only after IP called for it and the roll-in followed rather than preceded the lookout. Separation was maintained, but the clearing action was produced entirely by IP prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to fixation on the leader while awaiting the pitch out command, initially omitted the clearing scan of the turn direction. SP recognized the omission before rolling in, completed the lookout across the downwind leg and the base leg and confirmed the area was clear, then executed the pitch out without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP cleared the turn direction and the pattern before executing the pitch out and maintained the visual scan throughout the maneuver. The lookout covered the downwind and base legs while visual contact with the leader was retained. Separation from all pattern traffic was assured at every stage of the turn.
texts.4: SP maintained an exceptional visual scan throughout the pitch out, clearing the turn direction before the roll-in and continuing to sweep the pattern while holding visual contact with the leader. Every aircraft in the pattern was accounted for and reported without prompting. Attention was distributed with no lapse in either lookout or aircraft control.
texts.marginal: SP cleared the turn direction before the pitch out within standards, but the lookout was a single brief glance and the scan reverted immediately to the leader for the rest of the turn. The trend is a clearing action performed as a formality rather than as a continuous scan of the pattern. SP is expected to sustain the visual scan through the whole pitch out while retaining contact with the leader.

error_modes.label: DELAY BEFORE FOLLOWING THE LEADER TURN AND RESULTING SEPARATION

texts.0: SP, due to the delay before following Number 1 not being counted at all, did not stay behind the leader for the 2 to 3 seconds prescribed before turning to follow. The turn was started almost simultaneously with the leader and the separation at rollout was under 300 feet instead of the 500 to 1000 feet the delay is intended to produce. IP took the controls and widened the turn to rebuild a usable interval for the rejoin.
texts.1: SP, due to the count being started as the leader signal was given rather than as Number 1 actually began the turn, did not hold the prescribed delay before following. The delay came out close to one second and the separation at rollout finished at the bottom edge of the 500 to 1000 foot band. It was accepted only after IP called for more bank in the turn, so the interval remained usable but was produced by the prompt and not by SP own timing.
texts.2: SP, due to the delay being judged by feel instead of being counted, initially turned after little more than one second and set up a separation trend toward the short side. SP recognized the early start, varied the bank in the second half of the turn and rolled out with the separation inside the 500 to 1000 foot band. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP stayed visual on Number 1 and delayed 2 to 3 seconds as briefed before turning to follow. The separation at rollout fell squarely inside the 500 to 1000 feet that the standard delay is intended to produce. No adjustment beyond the normal spacing check was needed.
texts.4: SP held the briefed delay precisely, staying visual on Number 1 throughout and beginning the turn exactly at the end of the count. The separation at rollout sat in the middle of the 500 to 1000 foot band and required no adjustment at any point in the turn. The interval was ideal for the rejoin practice that followed.
texts.marginal: SP applied the briefed delay before following Number 1 within standards, but the count was consistently short and every rollout finished near 500 feet of separation. The trend is an anticipation of the leader turn that leaves the interval at the minimum end of the band on each repetition. SP is expected to stay visual and hold the full 2 to 3 second delay, and the briefed 5 to 7 seconds when the extended 1500 to 2000 foot spacing is called for, so that the separation is generated by the delay itself.

error_modes.label: SPACING ADJUSTMENT WITH BANK AND BACK STICK PRESSURE AFTER 90 DEGREES OF TURN

texts.0: SP, due to the pitchout being flown as a fixed bank turn with no reassessment once the leader stabilized, did not vary bank and back stick pressure after approximately 90 degrees of turn to attain the desired spacing. The interval collapsed through the second half of the turn and no adjustment was attempted before the rollout. IP took the controls, unloaded and widened the turn to rebuild the interval on the downwind leg.
texts.1: SP, due to the spacing being judged only at the rollout instead of at the 90 degree point, did not adjust bank and back stick pressure while the turn could still be used to build the interval. The separation finished at the very edge of what the pattern allows and was salvaged only after IP called for more bank in the turn. The interval was restored, but the adjustment came from the prompt and not from SP own assessment.
texts.2: SP, due to back stick pressure being held constant through the whole turn, initially carried the pitchout past the 90 degree point with the interval developing short. SP assessed the picture in the second half of the turn, varied bank and back stick pressure as the technique prescribes and had the desired spacing established before the rollout, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP assessed the developing interval at approximately 90 degrees of turn and varied bank and back stick pressure to attain the desired spacing. The adjustment was small and applied while the turn still had the geometry to produce it, so the rollout occurred at the briefed range. Nothing further was needed on the downwind leg.
texts.4: SP worked the spacing continuously from the 90 degree point, blending bank and back stick pressure so that the desired range was reached exactly as the wings came level. The corrections were so small as to be barely perceptible and the interval matched the briefed figure throughout. No adjustment at all was required after the rollout.
texts.marginal: SP varied bank and back stick pressure to attain the desired spacing within standards, but the adjustment was always started well past the 90 degree point and had to be made with a large late bank change. The interval finished acceptable on every repetition while remaining at the edge of the briefed range. SP is expected to begin working the spacing at approximately 90 degrees of turn so that only small inputs are needed to arrive at the correct range.

error_modes.label: ROLLOUT POSITION AND SHIP WIDTH SIGHT PICTURE ON NUMBER 1

texts.0: SP, due to the rollout being flown to a wings level attitude with no reference to where Number 1 sat in the canopy, did not roll out behind and slightly below the leader with Number 1 placed 1 to 2 ship widths above the horizon. The leader finished below the nose and offset to one side, leaving SP high and outside the trail geometry with the leader hard to hold visually. IP took the controls and repositioned the aircraft behind and below Number 1.
texts.1: SP, due to the sight picture being judged against the horizon alone rather than against the position of Number 1 on it, did not achieve the prescribed rollout position. The leader ended level with the horizon and SP was left co-altitude instead of slightly below, at the outer limit of a workable trail position. The picture was corrected only after IP called for a descent behind the leader.
texts.2: SP, due to the descent below the leader being started only at the rollout, initially placed Number 1 close to the horizon instead of 1 to 2 ship widths above it. SP recognized the flat picture immediately, eased down behind the leader and reestablished the prescribed rollout position before the ready call. No IP intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP rolled out behind and slightly below Number 1 with the leader placed 1 to 2 ship widths above the horizon as the technique prescribes. The sight picture was built during the turn rather than after it, so the position was correct as the wings came level. Visual contact with the leader was retained throughout.
texts.4: SP arrived at the rollout with Number 1 sitting squarely in the middle of the 1 to 2 ship width band above the horizon and the aircraft precisely in trail and slightly below. The picture was established progressively through the second half of the turn and needed no adjustment once level. Visual contact and the trail geometry were held without any apparent effort.
texts.marginal: SP rolled out behind and slightly below Number 1 within an acceptable position, but on every repetition the leader sat at the two ship width edge of the band and drifted toward the nose. The trend is a rollout flown slightly too low and too far back, so the picture has to be remade before the rejoin. SP is expected to place Number 1 in the middle of the prescribed band as the wings come level.

error_modes.label: READY CALL AT THE DESIRED RANGE

texts.0: SP, due to the range being watched with no intention of transmitting until the leader asked, did not call ready on reaching the desired range after the pitchout. The element stayed in trail with the interval opening and no rejoin could be directed, because Number 1 had no confirmation that the range had been achieved. IP made the call and then took the controls to close the interval that had built up in the meantime.
texts.1: SP, due to the call being withheld until the aircraft was perfectly stabilized rather than made at the desired range, did not report ready at the correct point. The transmission came several seconds late with the interval already at the outer limit for a rejoin, and only after IP prompted for the call. The rejoin was then directed normally, but the initiative was IP.
texts.2: SP, due to attention being absorbed entirely by the trail position, initially passed the desired range without transmitting. SP recognized the omission within a couple of seconds and made the ready call in standard terminology while the interval was still correct. The rejoin was directed with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP called ready on reaching the desired range, in standard terminology and with the aircraft stabilized in trail. The call was made at the point the range was achieved, so Number 1 could slow to the rejoin airspeed and direct the rejoin without delay. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP made the ready call exactly as the desired range was reached, with the aircraft stabilized behind and slightly below the leader. The phraseology was standard, brief and unambiguous, and the rejoin followed immediately. Radio discipline was faultless through the whole sequence.
texts.marginal: SP called ready at the desired range within standards, but on each repetition the call came after a noticeable pause and the interval had already grown beyond the briefed one. The trend is a report that lags the achieved range instead of coinciding with it. SP is expected to transmit the call as the desired range is reached so that the rejoin begins from the briefed interval.

error_modes.label: CLEARING NOT SACRIFICED TO PRECISE ALTITUDE OR AN EXACT 180 DEGREE TURN

texts.0: SP, due to the pitchout being flown to an exact 180 degrees and to a rigidly held altitude with the cross-check locked on the instruments, sacrificed clearing to maintain precise altitude control and an exact turn. The head stayed down from the roll-in to the rollout and nothing outside the aircraft was checked at any point of the maneuver. IP called the traffic in the pattern and took the controls to reestablish separation.
texts.1: SP, due to the exact 180 degrees of turn being treated as inviolable, sacrificed the lookout in order to hold the heading and the altitude precisely. The clearing scan was reduced to the bare minimum acceptable and was resumed only after IP called for the head to come up. Separation was never in doubt, but the priority was restored by IP and not by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to the altimeter being chased through the first quarter of the turn, initially let the clearing scan lapse in favour of precise altitude control. SP recognized the misplaced priority early, accepted a slight climb for energy management as the technique permits and kept the scan outside for the remainder of the pitchout, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP did not sacrifice clearing to maintain precise altitude control or an exact 180 degree turn. Slight variations in altitude and in the degrees of turn were accepted for energy management and area orientation, exactly as the technique allows, while the parameters stayed inside tolerance. The pattern was cleared continuously through the maneuver.
texts.4: SP kept clearing as the first priority throughout the pitchout while still holding the altitude and the turn essentially on the briefed values. The degrees of turn were adjusted deliberately for area orientation and the small altitude variations accepted were explained on the debrief as energy management. Neither the lookout nor the parameters suffered.
texts.marginal: SP did not sacrifice clearing to precise altitude control within standards, but on every repetition the scan tightened noticeably as the heading approached the 180 degree point. The trend is a priority that reverses under the pressure of finishing the turn exactly. SP is expected to accept the small adjustments in altitude and degrees of turn that the technique permits and to keep the lookout continuous through the whole pitchout.

error_modes.label: DECELERATION WITH POWER AND SPEED BRAKE WHEN DIRECTED TO TAKE SPACING

texts.0: SP, due to the take spacing direction being answered with a maneuver alone and no power reduction or speed brake, did not generate any deceleration relative to Number 1. The range barely changed and the aircraft was still practically in the formation position when the leader expected a trail interval. IP reduced the power, extended the speed brake and built the required range.
texts.1: SP, due to the power being reduced in small steps rather than to a setting that would actually produce a deceleration, did not build the range at a usable rate after being directed to take spacing. The range was still short of the briefed one at the end of the maneuver and increased only after IP called for the speed brake. The interval was eventually achieved, but through IP prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial power reduction that was insufficient for the range required, initially opened the interval more slowly than the briefed profile allowed. SP recognized the slow rate, added speed brake and completed the deceleration in good time, reaching the desired range and making the ready call without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP took spacing with a power reduction and speed brake used together, opening the range at a controlled rate to the briefed value. The deceleration was stopped as the desired range was reached, so the interval stabilized instead of continuing to grow. The aircraft was in trail at the briefed range for the rejoin.
texts.4: SP took spacing with a deceleration judged so accurately that the range stopped growing exactly at the briefed value. Power and speed brake were applied together and then reset, leaving the aircraft stabilized in trail with no overshoot. The interval was ideal for the rejoin that followed.
texts.marginal: SP took spacing within standards, but each time the deceleration was carried a little too far and the range finished at the outer edge of what the rejoin allows. The trend is a power reduction and speed brake extension that are removed late rather than anticipated. SP is expected to begin resetting the power before the desired range is reached so that the interval stabilizes on the briefed value.

error_modes.label: S TURNS FOR SPACING BEHIND AND BELOW NUMBER 1 PROP WASH

texts.0: SP, due to the S turns for spacing being flown level with and directly behind Number 1, did not keep the maneuver behind and below the leader prop wash. The aircraft was flown through the wash repeatedly, with sharp uncommanded rolls each time and the leader lost from view during the disturbance. IP took the controls, descended clear of the wash and reestablished a stable trail position.
texts.1: SP, due to the vertical displacement below the leader being allowed to wash out as the S turns developed, did not keep clear of Number 1 prop wash. The aircraft clipped the wash on each reversal and the position was corrected only after IP called for a descent. Spacing was achieved, but the whole maneuver was flown on the edge of the wash and the correction came from IP.
texts.2: SP, due to the first S turn being started before descending below the leader, initially flew into the edge of the prop wash and felt a light roll disturbance. SP eased the aircraft lower at once and flew the remaining reversals behind and below Number 1 as the technique describes, completing the spacing maneuver without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP took spacing with a series of S turns flown behind and below Number 1 prop wash, keeping the aircraft clear of the disturbance throughout. Each reversal was made with visual contact on the leader retained and the range building steadily. The desired interval was reached with the aircraft stable.
texts.4: SP flew the S turns for spacing precisely behind and below the leader, never entering the prop wash and never losing the visual on Number 1. The reversals were smooth and symmetric and the range grew at an even rate to the briefed value. The technique was applied exactly as described.
texts.marginal: SP kept the S turns behind and below Number 1 within standards, but the aircraft skimmed the top of the prop wash on the reversals and the resulting jolts were absorbed rather than avoided. The trend is a vertical offset that is only just sufficient and shrinks as the maneuver progresses. SP is expected to establish and hold a clear displacement below the leader wash before starting the S turns.
